jumbotron.body_text: Predicting the popularity of Trinidad dancehall songs in the US Market.

why_build_this.body_text: I've been a big fan of both trinidad dancehall (trinibad) and hip-hop music. I found it interesting how similar these genres are, both thematically and musically. Given that hip-hop was the dominating genre in the US, I started wondering how that market might respond to trinidad dancehall?.

challenges.body_text:
A first challenge was finding out what data even existed and how could I fetch that en-masse to create a dataset rich enough to explore. After some research, I found the Spotify API docs and that got me started on the ETL pipeline.

I did some initial exploring but then life happened and this project got parked for ~ 2 years. This was the second challenge i.e. figuring out how to continue developing in an older codebase.

learnings.body_text:
This was a good exercise in the end-to-end model development process minus deployment, but my day-to-day at work was mainly on the MLOps side, so this was a good opportunity to hone my modelling skills.

More great learnings came from setting up a fully local agentic workflow. which did a good job at accelerating the process.

body_text:
Being able to delegate tasks to a model while working on other things has been a great part of my daily workflow in work so I wanted a way to replicate that for personal projects while keeping costs low.

Luckily, I had also recently bought a new laptop with some decent specs and decided to try running it locally. I initially started with ollama and downloaded a few open source models - gemma, qwen and bonsai. However, this setup resulted in the models performing terribly in terms of correctness but also latency.

A few days of youtube vids, docs and ai mode - I switched to LM Studio with qwen-3.5 9B + opencode for agentic coding tasks and qwen-2.5-coder-1.5B-instruct for autocomplete. These models take ~ 8 GB VRAM with a 24k context and ~ 950 MB with an 8192 context respectively. They worked okay but still ran into issues due to running out of context, especially the agentic coding one.

The main breakthrough came through better managing the context for the model for example through maintaining an AGENTS.md to keep track of important things about the repo so the model doesn't have to look those up everytime.

Another method was through using skills to manage context. Referencing Juptyer notebooks using @ tended to brick the model as the file (a very heavy json with images) would exceed the context. The solution here was to create a skill to safely read notebook chunks so that the model could load these lazily.

Since that, I've been able to use the model for organizing various comments and helping with generating better docs. It currently does a good job when reading and planning but sometimes get stuck when trying to execute so this is still a work in progress, but learning more after each setback is an exciting journey.

jumbotron.body_text: Explore the long-term behaviour of various Roulette betting strategies.

why_build_this.body_text: My cousins operated a roulette machine in their bar. They would monitor the numbers throughout the day and then play large sums for certain combinations for example, if 0 was played in the previous round, they would play 31 as they said it was almost sure. Assuming the draws are random, this did not make sense to me so I conceptualized this simulator after learning about Monte Carlo Simulations and then built it 2 years later.

challenges.body_text:
This was my first attempt to properly use an Object-Oriented (OO) design and practice Test Driven Development. Setting up the automated tests with Github Actions also was an obstacle.

A fun fact: I built 90% of this while on a plane to Trinidad.

learnings.body_text: Writing tests beforehand was a game changer. It allowed me to really think about the solution before and not while I was implementing it. This let me break larger functionality into unit functions which made developing much easier and I moved away from a pure OO paradigm into a more functional paradigm where classes are used for representing data, but behaviour is handled by functions.

jumbotron.body_text: An online application for real estate agents to nurture prospective clients via SMS conversations.

why_build_this.body_text: At Select Realty Marketing, the main service is optimizing lead generation for real estate agents. As more agents joined, the current spreadsheet-based approach did not scale. We needed a way to manage and nurture prospects easily and for multiple agents.

challenges.body_text: This project was my first journey into full-stack development. The first obstacle was building an Express server to fetch data from our CRM (MailChimp). The next obstacle involved sending and receiving SMS messages and displaying them to an interface in real-time using Twilio’s API.

learnings.body_text: This project was my first exposure to cloud deployments and proper version control through Heroku and Github. I spent a lot more time doing back-end related work and developed a good foundation on REST API design and simple relational database operations like joins and filtering.

jumbotron.body_text: A real-time list of printers maintained by the Arts Computing Office at the University of Waterloo organized by department, building and model.

why_build_this.body_text: Printer related tickets made up near 40% of issues coming to the help desk. Most often, staff at the Faculty of Arts had trouble connecting to (or finding) their department printers and the Arts Computing Office had difficulty keeping track of its printers.

challenges.body_text: This project was the first web-related work I’d ever done so the main challenges were learning the stack - HTML, CSS & JavaScript, developing with accessibility in mind, and learning how to leverage PowerShell as a back-end.

learnings.body_text: This project made me fall in love with programming. I became comfortable with scripting in PowerShell and was ready to level up my web-development skills as I now had the foundations for HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

body_text: Accessibility is a top priority within the University’s design principles. The website needed to be compliant to at least a level of AA based on the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.0 (w3.org)

The main implication on this solution was that the site needed to be structured in a way such that screen readers can easily describe the on-screen content so that users can interact with the site using solely their keyboard.

This is done on a smaller scale through including alternate descriptions of images or tables. On a larger scale, designing with accessibility in mind reinforces good user experience (UX) principles by ensuring that the flow of your site is intuitive and functional.

For example, the search bar was placed at the top left of the non-generic content (The header and navbar) because this is usually the starting point for reading English, which reads from left to right, and searching for printers is the most used feature of the website.

This project introduced me to the WCAG 2.0 and also to the idea of user-centric design. It sparked a curiosity into UX and general user interface (UI) design principles which still fascinate me up to today.
The project is deployed as a PowerShell script, scheduled to run daily, on the Arts Computing Office’s (ACO) servers.
The script has a few responsibilities like:

• Fetching a table of printers from our print server and organizing them into an appropriate format.
  • Generating an HTML file containing the structure and content of the web page.
  • Generating a CSS file for styling according to the University of Waterloo design standards.
  • Generating a JavaScript file which powers the interactivity of the web page.
Here, a user is anyone that wants to print something in any building within the Faculty of Arts.

Through this site, users were able to easily locate the printer nearest to them. Staff members with work laptops were able to quickly install their department printers by using the “Installation Help” button and effortlessly copy-paste the printer’s path, required for their installation.
On our end, we had much less printer-related issues and were able to spend more time on our main project - upgrading staff laptops from Windows 7 to Windows 10.

Since it is deployed within the Arts Computing Office’s servers, users would need to be connected to the campus WiFi or use the University's VPN. If you meet that criteria, you can view the site at Printing, scanning, copying | Arts Computing Office (uwaterloo.ca).
